algorithm: Token bucket with continuous time-based refill

classes.desc: Deterministic clock for the demo: time moves only when advance() is called.
classes.name: FakeClock

classes.desc: Token-bucket rate limiter with continuous refill and an injectable clock.

data_flow_ascii:
seeded arrival schedule -> FakeClock.advance -> TokenBucket._refill
TokenBucket.allow -> ALLOW (token consumed) or DENY (bucket empty)
allowed/denied counters -> stats() -> printed table + admission rate
description_sentence: A token-bucket rate limiter that refills continuously over time and reports allow/deny decisions for a scripted request schedule.
failure_note: Invalid rate or capacity raises ValueError at construction; the demo never sleeps, so it cannot stall on timing.

functions.name: build_parser

functions.name: main

label: rate limiter
output_shape: Prints a per-request table (request number, timestamp, tokens, ALLOW/DENY) plus the admission-rate summary.
pitch_sentence: I built a {topic} that smooths bursty traffic with a token bucket and shows exactly which requests get admitted or denied.

qa.a: On every call, tokens increase by elapsed_seconds * rate_per_sec, capped at capacity, so refills are continuous rather than per-tick.
A FakeClock makes the arrival schedule fully deterministic, so the allow/deny table is identical on every run.
qa.q: Why does the demo use a fake clock?

qa.a: A fixed window can admit 2x the rate at window boundaries; the bucket smooths bursts because tokens accrue gradually.
qa.q: How would this differ from a fixed-window limiter?

resume_bullet_template: Built a {topic} in Python using the token-bucket algorithm with an injectable clock for deterministic testing.
run_notes: --rate, --capacity, and --requests override the demo configuration from @@TOPIC_PARAMS@@.
scaling_note: Single-process bucket; a distributed service would need a shared store like Redis so all instances draw from one bucket.
storage_note: In-memory only: token balance and counters reset when the process exits.
tradeoff_note: Continuous refill is smoother than fixed windows but needs a monotonic clock; float token math is approximate by design.
